stem: A stadium app routes every incoming fan message to one of six queues (tickets, parking, concessions and so on) before a human or bot handles it. It processes millions of short messages on game days, routing must add almost no delay, and evals show every tier classifies these messages accurately. Which model choice best fits?

options.text: Use the most capable tier, so routing quality stays high when unusual messages arrive.
options.explanation: The evals already show every tier routes accurately. The top tier adds latency and cost without a measured gain.

options.text: Use a Haiku-tier model, which is the fastest and cheapest tier for high-volume routing.
options.explanation: Correct. Haiku fits classification and routing at high volume with tight latency, and the evals confirm it does the job.

options.text: Use an Opus-tier model at maximum effort, so each message gets the deepest reasoning.
options.explanation: Maximum effort on the larger tier adds the most latency and cost, for a task that doesn't need it.

options.text: Use the tier with the largest context window, because game-day volume will be very high.
options.explanation: Volume is about throughput and rate limits, not context-window size. Each message is short.

stem: A front office is building an agent that spends hours reading contracts, cap tables and scouting reports to propose multi-player trades. The task needs complex reasoning, and the team has no evals yet. They also want to keep costs reasonable once the agent works. Which strategy best fits?

options.text: Start on the smallest tier and move up only when users complain about the trade proposals.
options.explanation: Efficiency-first fits simple, high-volume work. For complex agentic reasoning, user complaints are a slow and costly way to find the capability gap.

options.text: Pick the tier with the lowest price per token and keep it as long as the agent finishes its runs.
options.explanation: Finishing a run isn't the same as producing good trades. Price per token ignores retries and the cost of bad output.

options.text: Run every tier in production at once and let the agent choose its own model for each step.
options.explanation: This multiplies cost and complexity before anything is measured, and caches don't carry across models.

options.text: Start capability-first on Opus, build evals, then lower effort or tier while evals pass.
options.explanation: Correct. For complex agentic work, get it working on a strong model first, then use evals to step effort or tier down where quality holds.

stem: A recap generator runs well on an Opus-tier model at its default effort, but the monthly bill is higher than planned. A team member proposes switching the whole feature to a Sonnet-tier model right away. Evals exist for the feature. What should the team try first?

options.text: Lower effort on the current model and re-run the evals to see if quality holds.
options.explanation: Correct. Effort trades intelligence against latency and cost within one model, and the docs call it often a better lever than switching models. Measure it before changing tiers.

options.text: Switch to the Sonnet-tier model right away, since per-token prices are lower on that tier.
options.explanation: This may work, but it skips a cheaper experiment and changes many behaviors at once. Try lower effort and measure first.

options.text: Cut max_tokens in half on every request so each recap uses fewer output tokens.
options.explanation: A tighter hard cap risks truncated recaps and retries, which can raise cost per finished recap.

options.text: Add a temperature setting of 0 so each recap is shorter and more focused.
options.explanation: Temperature doesn't control length, and current models reject non-default sampling values.

stem: A team compares two tiers for drafting contract summaries. The smaller tier costs a fraction as much per token, but on the eval set about a third of its drafts fail validation and need a retry or a lawyer's fix. The larger tier rarely fails. Which approach best decides the choice?

options.text: Choose the smaller tier, because its per-token price is lower and retries are cheap anyway.
options.explanation: Per-token price ignores retries, extra turns and the cost of human fixes, which may outweigh the savings.

options.text: Choose the larger tier, because a more capable model is always the better choice for legal text.
options.explanation: "Always use the most capable model" ignores cost and latency. The choice should come from measurement.

options.text: Compare the cost per completed, validated summary for each tier, including retries and human fixes.
options.explanation: Correct. Judge models by cost per completed task, including retries, extra turns and failure handling, not by price per token.

options.text: Choose whichever tier has the larger context window, since contracts can be long documents.
options.explanation: Context window size doesn't address the failure rate. Both tiers may fit the documents.

stem: A team moves an older Haiku 4.5 integration to the newest Haiku model. The old code sends temperature 0.2 and ends the messages with an assistant turn containing "{" to force JSON output. Both now cause 400 errors. Which two changes should they make? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Remove the temperature setting and steer consistency with instructions and examples.
options.explanation: Correct. Current models reject non-default sampling values. Prompting, examples and validation replace them.

options.text: Add a date suffix to the model ID so the request pins the older request behavior.
options.explanation: A model ID selects a model; it doesn't restore old request rules. The newest model still rejects these parameters.

options.text: Keep the prefill but shorten it to a single space so validation accepts it.
options.explanation: Any final assistant turn used as a prefill is rejected on current models, whatever its content.

options.text: Replace the prefill with structured outputs that enforce the JSON schema.
options.explanation: Correct. Structured outputs guarantee schema-valid JSON, which is what the prefill was approximating.

options.text: Raise temperature to 1.0 so the request falls back to the older defaults.
options.explanation: Sending sampling parameters is what triggers the error. The fix is to remove them, not to change the value.

stem: A broadcaster's compliance lead worries that because their code uses a model ID without a date, Anthropic could silently swap in a new model and change recap behavior mid-season. Which statement best addresses the concern?

options.text: The ID refers to a fixed snapshot; behavior changes when they change the ID, so track deprecation dates.
options.explanation: Correct. Model IDs are pinned snapshots, not moving pointers. Nothing changes until the team changes the ID, but they must plan for the model's retirement date.

options.text: The ID always points to the latest release, so they should add a date suffix to pin it in place.
options.explanation: Current IDs aren't moving aliases, and constructing date suffixes for current models isn't valid.

options.text: The ID is updated weekly, so they should run evals every Monday to catch behavior changes.
options.explanation: No weekly swap happens. Evals belong at deliberate upgrade points.

options.text: The ID never retires, so the team can keep the same model for as long as the product exists.
options.explanation: Models are deprecated and retired on published schedules. Ignoring retirement dates risks an outage.

stem: A league data team plans to move its player-comparison feature to a newer model release next month. Which two steps belong in a safe upgrade plan? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Reuse the old effort setting unchanged, since effort levels mean the same thing across releases.
options.explanation: Effort defaults differ between models and levels can be recalibrated between releases, so the old setting may behave differently.

options.text: Skip evals if the new model is in the same tier, since same-tier releases behave identically.
options.explanation: Releases within a tier change defaults, parameters and behavior. Evals are how you find out.

options.text: Recount tokens with the new model and revisit max_tokens limits and cost estimates.
options.explanation: Correct. A newer tokenizer can produce more tokens for the same text, which affects caps and budgets.

options.text: Keep the old request code as is, since API parameters don't change between model releases.
options.explanation: Releases have removed options such as sampling parameters, prefill and thinking budgets. Request shapes must be checked against the migration guide.

options.text: Re-run the evals and re-tune effort starting from the new model's default level.
options.explanation: Correct. A safe upgrade reads the migration guide, updates request shapes, then measures quality and re-tunes effort on the new model.

stem: A developer needs to know which models available to the organization support adaptive thinking and image input before choosing one for a new scouting feature. A blog post from last year lists some models. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Use the list from last year's blog post, since model capabilities don't change after release.
options.explanation: New models arrive and old ones retire. A year-old list can be wrong about what's available.

options.text: Send a test request to each model with every feature enabled and see which ones fail.
options.explanation: Trial and error wastes calls and confuses capability gaps with other errors.

options.text: Query the Models API, which reports each model's capabilities, and check the models overview.
options.explanation: Correct. The Models API returns current models with their capabilities, so the choice rests on live data rather than memory.

options.text: Assume all models support every feature, since all current models share one request format.
options.explanation: Older models, such as Haiku 4.5, support only the fixed-budget thinking mode. Support varies by model.

stem: A league's research agent runs for hours, synthesizing years of rule changes and injury data into policy proposals. On the team's eval set, an Opus-tier model at high effort still misses key interactions between rules. Latency doesn't matter, and the budget allows a higher per-token price if quality improves. Which next step best fits?

options.text: Move to a Haiku-tier model and run it several times, keeping the most common answer
options.explanation: Repeating a less capable model doesn't close a reasoning gap that a stronger tier already shows.

options.text: Evaluate the Fable tier on the same eval set and adopt it if it closes the gap
options.explanation: Correct. Fable is the most capable widely released tier, meant for long agent sessions and deep research when Opus at high effort still falls short. Latency and price are explicitly acceptable here.

options.text: Lower Opus's effort so it completes more research passes in the same time
options.explanation: Lower effort trades quality for speed and cost, which is the opposite of what this team needs.

options.text: Keep the current setup and add more instructions telling Claude to consider rule interactions
options.explanation: Prompt work is worth trying, but the scenario says the eval gap persists at high effort and the budget allows a stronger tier. Measuring that tier is the direct test.

stem: After moving a playbook-summary feature from Claude Opus 4.6 to a newer Opus release, the team notices that `usage.input_tokens` is higher for identical prompts, a few summaries now stop with `max_tokens`, and the monthly cost forecast is off. The prompts haven't changed. What best explains this, and what should they do?

options.text: The newer model writes longer summaries; add "be concise" to the prompt and keep the old limits
options.explanation: This doesn't explain why input tokens rose for identical prompts, which points at how text is counted, not at output style.

options.text: The usage numbers are wrong during the rollout; wait a billing cycle for them to settle
options.explanation: Usage reflects how the request was tokenized. Waiting leaves the truncation and the bad forecast in place.

options.text: Prompt caching broke during the migration; add more cache breakpoints to bring token counts down
options.explanation: Caching changes how input is billed, not how many input tokens the text contains, and it doesn't affect output truncation.

options.text: A new tokenizer counts the same text as more tokens; recount and fix limits and estimates
options.explanation: Correct. The same text can produce more tokens under a newer tokenizer, so limits and estimates tuned for the old model need re-baselining.

stem: A stats-extraction service forces a tool call with `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "record_stats"}`, purely to get JSON back. After an upgrade to Claude Opus 5.5, every request fails with a 400 saying this `tool_choice` type isn't supported for the model. Which fix best fits?

options.text: Switch to `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}`, which still guarantees that some tool gets called
options.explanation: `any` is also a forced choice, and it is rejected on this model as well.

options.text: End the messages with an assistant turn starting with `{` so Claude continues the JSON
options.explanation: Assistant prefill is rejected on current models too, so this trades one 400 for another.

options.text: Use structured outputs, or `auto` with a `strict` tool plus an instruction to call it
options.explanation: Correct. Structured outputs suits a call that only existed to get JSON. Otherwise `auto` plus `strict: true` keeps arguments schema-valid while the prompt steers Claude to call the tool.

options.text: Pin the service to the previous model indefinitely so the request shape never has to change
options.explanation: This postpones the change until that model is retired, and the service then fails with no time to migrate.

stem: A team proposes an Opus-tier orchestrator that hands the reading of 200 game logs to Haiku-tier worker sub-agents, to cut cost compared with running everything on Opus. Each worker receives the same long league-rules preamble. Which TWO considerations should shape the decision? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Compare cost per completed task against the simpler option of one model at a lower effort level
options.explanation: Correct. A single capable model at lower effort is often competitive, and only measuring whole tasks shows which design really costs less.

options.text: Skip measurement, since a Haiku-tier worker is always cheaper overall than an Opus-tier one
options.explanation: Per-token price isn't per-task cost. Retries, extra turns and orchestration overhead can erase the difference.

options.text: The workers can reuse the orchestrator's cached copy of the preamble, so the preamble is nearly free
options.explanation: Caches are scoped to a model, so a cache written by the Opus orchestrator doesn't serve Haiku workers.

options.text: Prompt caches are model-scoped, so the preamble is cached separately for the worker model
options.explanation: Correct. Each model keeps its own cache. The design must account for writing and reading the preamble under the worker model.

options.text: Use a Fable-tier model for the workers so they never need the orchestrator to check their output
options.explanation: This raises cost on the highest-volume part of the system, the opposite of the stated goal.

stem: To cut costs, a team proposes a cascade: every request goes to Haiku first, and anything Haiku seems unsure about is retried on Opus. What should they measure before building it?

options.text: Nothing, because cascades always cost less than a single model.
options.explanation: Cascades can cost more once escalations and lost cache reuse are counted, so it has to be measured.

options.text: Only whether Haiku's answers sound confident, since that decides escalation.
options.explanation: How confident an answer sounds is a poor signal of whether it is correct. The decision needs task-level evaluation.

options.text: Haiku's cost per request alone, since that's where most traffic will go.
options.explanation: Cost per request ignores escalations, retries and lower-quality answers that need extra turns. Cost per completed task is the right measure.

options.text: The most capable model at a lower effort setting on the same tasks, compared by cost per completed task. It often matches the cascade, keeps one model's prompt cache and avoids the escalation logic.
options.explanation: Correct. Lower effort on a strong model is often cheaper overall than a cascade. A cascade also loses cache reuse across models and pays twice for the requests it escalates.

stem: A coaching app streams Claude's reasoning into a "How I got there" panel while the answer is prepared. After moving from Claude Opus 4.6 to a newer Opus model with adaptive thinking, the panel stays blank and users see a long pause before the answer. The thinking blocks still arrive, but their text is empty. Which change best fits?

options.text: Go back to a fixed thinking budget with budget_tokens, which always returns the full thinking text.
options.explanation: Newer Opus models reject budget_tokens with a 400. The empty text comes from a display default, not from the thinking mode.

options.text: Raise the effort level so the model thinks more and the thinking blocks fill with text again.
options.explanation: Effort changes how much the model thinks, not whether the thinking text is returned. The blocks would stay empty, just with more billed tokens.

options.text: Treat the empty blocks as a sign that thinking is now disabled and switch thinking back on.
options.explanation: The model did think; the empty blocks are the new default display, and thinking is still billed. Nothing needs to be switched back on.

options.text: Set the thinking display option to "summarized", since newer models omit thinking text by default.
options.explanation: Correct. On newer models the default display is omitted, a silent change from Opus 4.6, which returned summarized thinking. Opting into the summarized display restores the visible reasoning.

stem: A team moves a fan-moderation feature from a much older Claude model to a current one. Their code handles only the end_turn, max_tokens and tool_use stop reasons. Now a few responses arrive with HTTP 200 but show users an empty or cut-off reply, and nothing is logged as an error. Which change best fits?

options.text: Treat any HTTP 200 as a success and retry only the responses whose text is empty.
options.explanation: A status of 200 doesn't mean the model produced a normal answer. Retrying on empty text ignores the stop reason that explains what happened.

options.text: Check stop_reason first and add a branch for "refusal", with its own handling and logging.
options.explanation: Correct. Current models can stop with stop_reason "refusal", which older code paths don't expect. Checking stop_reason before reading content lets the app log it and show a deliberate message or fallback.

options.text: Raise max_tokens, because empty replies mean the answer was cut off by the output cap.
options.explanation: A cap-related stop would report stop_reason "max_tokens", which the code already handles. These responses carry a stop reason the code doesn't check.

options.text: Switch back to the older model for moderation, since current models return malformed replies.
options.explanation: The replies aren't malformed; the code is missing a stop reason. Older models also get retired, so moving back only postpones the fix.

stem: A league's archive service pins an exact model snapshot so recap behavior never changes, and the team plans to leave it untouched for several seasons. They receive a notice that the model is deprecated, with a retirement date. Which plan best fits?

options.text: Test the recommended replacement on their evals and migrate before the retirement date.
options.explanation: Correct. A deprecated model still works but has a retirement date, after which requests to it fail. Testing the replacement early and migrating in time avoids an outage.

options.text: Keep the pinned snapshot, since a pinned model ID is guaranteed to be served indefinitely.
options.explanation: Pinning prevents silent changes, but it doesn't keep a model available forever. Once a model is retired, requests to it fail.

options.text: Wait until requests start failing, then change the model ID to the newest one available.
options.explanation: Waiting guarantees an outage, and swapping IDs without testing risks broken request shapes and changed behavior.

options.text: Move to a cloud provider, where deprecated models remain available on the same schedule forever.
options.explanation: Partner platforms set their own retirement schedules, but models are still retired there. Switching platforms only moves the deadline.
